title: The Wavefunction Specifies the State of a System
lead: Quantum mechanics replaces the classical state, a point of position and momentum, with a wavefunction. Its square is a probability density, and that reading limits which functions can be wavefunctions.
objectives: Introduce the first postulate of quantum mechanics
notes: Adapted from Allan Adams, Matthew Evans and Barton Zwiebach (MIT OpenCourseWare, used with permission), under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

figures.original_caption: Examples of good wavefunctions, $\psi(x)$, (red, top) and corresponding probability densities, $P(x)$, (blue, bottom).

(4.1.2) This function is an invalid wavefunction since the amplitude is going to infinity over a region (the middle in this case). (4.1.3) This function is an invalid wavefunction since it is not a proper function (i. e., not one-to-one). (4.1.4) These functions are invalid wavefunctions. (left) The first derivative of a function gives its gradient at a given point, and it thus exists as long as the function is continuous - only if there is a break in the function is there a point at which its first derivative does not exist. (right) The second derivative of this wavefunction is discontinuous at the point indicated, where the gradient of the line changes by more than 180º. In practice, this requirement may be somewhat flexible, particularly if the potential energy of the system shows rapid changes with distance. (CC BY-NC; Ümit Kaya via LibreTexts)

exercises.prompt:
Determine if each of the following functions is acceptable as a wavefunction over the indicated regions:

  1. $\cos x$ over $(0,\infty)$
  2. $e^x$ over $(-\infty,\infty)$
  3. $e^{-x}$ over $[0,\infty)$
  4. $\tan \theta$ over $[0, 2\theta]$

answer.solution:
Solution a

This is not an acceptable wavefunction. It is single-valued across the entire range. There is a single value for each value of $x$. It is continuous over the defined limits of integration, as we can see from a plot given below. However, it is not square-integrable.

$$ \int_{0}^{\infty} | \cos(x) |^2 dx \; \xcancel{<} \; \infty $$

Solution b

This is not an acceptable wavefunction. Over the limits of integration from $-\infty$ to $\infty$, this function is not square-integrable. Note in the plot below, how the function is indefinite approaching the limits of $\infty$.

Solution c

This is an acceptable wavefunction over the given limits. It is finite over the given limits. It is continuous within given limits. It is single-valued. It is square-integrable with $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} | \Psi(x) |^2 dx = \frac{1}{2}$.

Solution d

This is not an acceptable wavefunction. It is discontinuous over the limits of integration.

footnotes.html: $k$ is the wavenumber, not the period. The period of $e^{ikx}$ in $x$ is $2\pi/k$.
The second line drops the constant $N$: it should read $|Ne^{ikx}|^2$, which the third line goes on to evaluate.
The interval is $[0, 2\pi]$, the range the key's plot of $\tan\theta$ covers.
$\Psi(x)$ here is the function under test, $e^{-x}$: $\int_0^\infty e^{-2x}\,dx = \tfrac{1}{2}$.
